items: Runs after the tool, before Claude reads
Can replace or add to the result
Example: unify dates and status codes

quiz.q: Policy says refunds over $500 need a human. Which approach guarantees compliance without blocking smaller refunds?
options: State the $500 limit clearly at the top of the system prompt
Remove the refund tool and route every refund to a human agent
A `PreToolUse` hook that denies refunds over $500 and redirects them
A `PostToolUse` hook that logs a warning when a refund exceeds $500

quiz.q: Three MCP tools return dates as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings and numeric codes. Claude sometimes orders events wrongly. What is the best fix?
options: A `PostToolUse` hook that converts every result to one format
A system-prompt legend that explains each tool's date format
A `PreToolUse` hook that blocks any tool returning non-ISO dates
Few-shot examples showing Claude how to compare mixed dates
quiz.why: Normalising results in a `PostToolUse` hook is deterministic. A legend or examples still leave Claude to interpret mixed formats.

quiz.q: Why can't a `PostToolUse` hook enforce a refund limit?
options: `PostToolUse` hooks cannot read the input the tool was called with
It runs after the tool has executed, so the refund has already happened
Only system prompts are allowed to make decisions about money
`PostToolUse` hooks only run for MCP tools, not for built-in ones
quiz.why: By the time a result exists the action is done. Stopping an action needs an interception hook that runs before the call.

quiz.q: What does a hook give you that a system-prompt rule does not?
options: Lower token cost, because the rule no longer sits in each request
Better tone and wording in Claude's replies to the customer
The ability for Claude to weigh up exceptions case by case
A deterministic guarantee, because the code runs on every call
quiz.why: Hooks are code that runs every time, so compliance is guaranteed. Prompt rules give only probabilistic compliance.

misconceptions.myth: Any hook can enforce a limit on an action.
misconceptions.fact: Only a hook that runs before the call can stop it. `PostToolUse` runs after the action has already happened.

misconceptions.myth: Explaining each tool's format in the prompt is as good as normalising it.
misconceptions.fact: Claude can still misread mixed formats. A `PostToolUse` hook converts them deterministically before Claude sees them.

misconceptions.myth: The safest way to stop large refunds is to remove the refund tool.
misconceptions.fact: That blocks legitimate refunds too. An interception hook blocks only the calls that break policy.

scenario.title: Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenario.story:
A subscription company's support agent used three MCP tools: billing, orders and shipping. Two problems surfaced in the same month.

First, a customer pushed hard for a $750 refund and got it, although the system prompt said refunds over $500 needed a human. Second, Claude told several customers their parcels shipped before they were ordered. The orders tool returned Unix timestamps, shipping returned ISO 8601 dates, and Claude compared them as if they matched.

An engineer suggested a `PostToolUse` hook to flag large refunds. A colleague pointed out that it would fire after the money had gone. Instead they added a `PreToolUse` hook on `mcp__billing__process_refund`. It denies any amount over 500 with the reason "Call escalate_to_human", and lets smaller refunds through.

For the dates, they added a `PostToolUse` hook on the order and shipping tools. It rewrites every timestamp into ISO 8601 and every status code into a word before Claude reads it. Both problems stopped.

plain: Big tasks have to be split into smaller ones, and the right way to split depends on the task. If the steps are always the same, use a fixed sequence. If you only find out what to do next by looking, use a plan that changes as you go. For large code reviews, look at each file on its own first, then do a separate pass that looks across files.
analogy: A car MOT follows the same checklist every time. A detective following leads does not. And proof-reading a book chapter by chapter catches typos, but you still need one read-through for plot holes that span chapters.

sections.h: Two ways to split a task
sections.body:
**Predictable work suits a fixed pipeline; open-ended work needs a plan that adapts.**

**Fixed sequential pipeline**, also called **prompt chaining**: a set series of steps, each its own prompt, often feeding the next.

- Fits work where the **same steps always apply**.
- Example: every pull request is checked for security, then performance, then error handling.
- It guarantees each mandatory step runs.

**Dynamic adaptive decomposition**: Claude plans, acts, learns something, and re-plans.

- Fits **open-ended** investigation where the next step depends on what you find.
- Example: "Find out why checkout got twice as slow last week."

Picking the wrong style fails in a predictable way. A pipeline cannot follow an unexpected lead. An open-ended agent may skip a check that was mandatory.

sections.h: Large reviews: local passes, then an integration pass
sections.body:
**Review each file on its own, then do a separate pass for how the files fit together.**

Reviewing 20 changed files in **one pass** spreads attention thin. Some files get a careful look and others a glance. This is **attention dilution**.

The better structure has two stages:

1. **Per-file local passes.** Review each file alone. These can run in parallel. They catch local bugs, such as a missing null check or an unsafe SQL query.
2. **Cross-file integration pass.** A separate pass that sees only how files connect: exported functions, signatures and call sites. It catches a function renamed in one file but still called by its old name in another.

You need both. Local passes alone miss cross-file breaks. One giant pass misses local detail.

**When you cannot plan everything upfront, map first and let the plan change.**

Take "add thorough tests to a legacy codebase". You do not know the code yet, so a fixed plan would be guesswork.

1. **Map the structure**: modules, entry points, dependencies.
2. **Find high-impact areas**: payment code, heavily used helpers, files with a history of bugs.
3. **Build a prioritised plan** from that map.
4. **Adapt as you learn.** If module A cannot be tested until shared helper B is untangled, move B up the list.

The plan is a living list, not a contract. Freezing it on day one would ignore exactly the dependencies that step 4 uncovers.

**Read the task for two clues: is it predictable, and does it span many files?**

- **Same steps every time?** Use a fixed pipeline. A CI review that must always check security is the classic case.
- **Next step depends on what you find?** Use adaptive decomposition. Incident investigations and codebase exploration fit here.
- **Many files?** Add per-file passes plus one integration pass, whichever style you chose.

These combine. A CI review can be a fixed chain of aspects, run per file, followed by an integration pass.

Do not reach for a more powerful agent or a bigger budget to fix a structure problem. A smarter reviewer in one pass still dilutes its attention, and an open-ended agent still might skip a mandatory check.

**Most failures come from one big pass or the wrong style for the task.**

- **One long prompt for a big review.** A longer, more detailed prompt does not fix diluted attention.
- **Per-file reviews only.** Fast and parallel, but a signature change that breaks three callers goes unnoticed.
- **A fixed pipeline for an investigation.** Step 4 says "check the database" even though step 2 already showed a CDN change was the cause.
- **An open-ended agent for a predictable review.** A bigger budget does not guarantee a security check every time. A fixed pipeline does.

The rule: **predictable → fixed pipeline; open-ended → adaptive plan; many files → per-file passes plus an integration pass.**

example.title: Worked example: a CI review pipeline with local and integration passes
example.code:
ASPECTS = ["security", "error handling", "performance"]   # always the same

def review_pr(changed_files, diff):
    findings = []
    # 1) Per-file local passes (can run in parallel)
    for f in changed_files:
        for aspect in ASPECTS:                            # fixed chain
            findings += ask_claude(
                f"Review ONLY {f.path} for {aspect}.\n{f.content}")

    # 2) Separate cross-file integration pass
    summary = summarise_interfaces(changed_files)  # signatures, exports, calls
    findings += ask_claude(
        "Given these interface changes across files, find mismatches: "
        "renamed functions, changed contracts, broken callers.\n" + summary)
    return findings
notes: The aspects are predictable and mandatory, so a fixed chain guarantees each one runs on every file.
Each local pass sees one file, which avoids attention dilution.
The integration pass is separate and focuses only on how files interact.
`summarise_interfaces` keeps the integration pass small: signatures and call sites, not every line.

labs.title: Review of a 15-file rename misses issues
labs.context: A CI review of a 15-file pull request that renames getUser to fetchUser keeps missing issues. Recent misses include an SQL injection in file 11 and a call to the old getUser name in file 14 that broke the build after merge.
labs.question: Which review structure should the pipeline use?

options.text: One review pass over all 15 files with a longer, more detailed prompt that demands line-by-line checks and cross-file consistency.
options.code:
"Review all 15 files below very carefully.
Check every line for bugs, security, style and
cross-file consistency. Be thorough.
<15 files pasted>"

trace.text: Detailed comments on files 1-4.
Brief comments on files 5-15.
Missed: SQL injection in file 11.
Missed: file 14 still calls getUser.

options.verdict: Attention diluted across all files.
options.why: One pass spreads attention thin across 15 files, so later files get shallow review. Trap: fixing attention dilution with a longer prompt instead of separate per-file and integration passes.

options.text: Per-file local review passes, followed by a separate integration pass over exports and call sites to catch cross-file breaks.
options.code:
1. for each file (parallel): local review
2. integration pass over interface summary:
   "Find renamed/removed symbols still
    referenced elsewhere and changed contracts."

trace.text: 15 local passes run in parallel.
File 11: SQL injection found.
Integration pass receives exports and call sites.
Integration: "file 14 line 32 calls getUser, which no longer exists."
Both issues reported before merge.

options.verdict: Catches local and cross-file issues.
options.why: Per-file passes give each file focused attention, which catches the SQL injection. The separate integration pass looks across files, which catches the stale getUser call.

options.text: Per-file review passes run in parallel, one for each changed file, with all findings merged into a single PR comment.
options.code:
for each file in PR (in parallel):
    "Review this one file for bugs and security."
merge all findings
post merged findings to the PR

trace.text: 15 parallel reviews start.
File 11: "SQL injection in buildQuery()". Caught.
File 14: "Looks fine." (getUser is not defined in this file, but the reviewer cannot see that.)
Build fails after merge: getUser is undefined.

options.verdict: Local bugs caught, cross-file break missed.
options.why: Per-file passes alone miss problems that span files, such as the stale getUser call in file 14. Trap: right pattern, wrong scope; the separate integration pass is missing.

options.text: One review pass that also loads the whole repository, so the reviewer has full context for every changed file.
options.code:
claude -p "Review this PR. Full repository is
  included for context." \
  --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" \
  --output-format json

trace.text: Prompt: 15 changed files + 600 repository files.
Comments mostly on files 1 to 3.
Missed: SQL injection in file 11.
Missed: file 14 still calls getUser.

options.verdict: More context, even thinner attention.
options.why: Right pattern, wrong problem: the reviewer lacks focus, not context. Adding the whole repository spreads attention further, so local bugs are missed more often.

labs.takeaway: Many files: per-file local passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass.

labs.title: Fixed pipeline cannot find a memory leak
labs.context: A team uses an agent to investigate why a legacy order service's memory climbs until it crashes every 2 days. The agent runs a fixed pipeline: read the error logs, grep for OutOfMemory, read the 5 most-mentioned files, then summarise. It keeps blaming one request handler, while heap data points to a cache inside a shared library the pipeline never opens.
labs.question: How should the investigation be structured?

options.text: Extend the pipeline with extra fixed steps that also read every shared library and the latest heap dump on every run.
options.code:
pipeline:
  - read: logs/error.log
  - grep: OutOfMemory
  - read: top_5_mentioned_files
  - read: libs/**        # new
  - read: heap.hprof     # new
  - summarise

trace.text: Step 5 (new): read all 40 shared-library files.
Notices a large cache but the pipeline moves to "summarise".
Summary mentions the cache once; eviction bug not traced.

options.verdict: Catches this leak; misses the next one.
options.why: It now covers this lead but cannot follow whatever the next finding reveals. Trap: a fixed pipeline for open-ended investigation, which needs steps chosen from what is discovered.

options.text: Run per-file analysis passes over the whole service, followed by one cross-file integration pass over the results.

trace.text: 310 per-file passes start.
Integration pass: "No obvious cross-file defects."
3 hours of tokens; the cache eviction bug is not found.

options.verdict: Thorough review, wrong kind of task.
options.why: Right pattern, wrong problem: per-file plus integration passes suit reviewing a known set of changes. A leak hunt needs to follow evidence, not scan every file equally.

options.text: Spawn five parallel subagents, each assigned one fixed hypothesis about the leak, and take the majority verdict.

trace.text: Hypotheses: handler, ORM, thread pool, logging, sessions.
3 of 5 subagents: "probable cause: request handler".
Majority verdict is wrong; leak continues.

options.verdict: Five guesses; the right one was not on the list.
options.why: Over-engineered, and still fixed upfront: the hypotheses are chosen before any evidence. None of them covered the shared-library cache, so the vote picks a wrong cause.

options.text: Let the agent decompose dynamically: map the service, form hypotheses, and pick each next step from what it finds.
options.code:
Agent goal:
"Find why memory grows until the service crashes.
Start by mapping the service and checking heap data.
Form hypotheses, test the most likely one next,
and revise the plan after each finding."

trace.text: Maps the service and reads heap summary: 70% retained by PriceCache.
Next step chosen: open libs/pricing/cache.py.
Cache has no eviction; keys include a timestamp.
Confirms with a 10-minute load test; memory grows linearly.
Root cause reported with a fix plan.

options.verdict: Follows the evidence to the real cause.
options.why: Open-ended investigation needs dynamic, adaptive decomposition because the next step depends on what is found. The plan changes once the heap data points at the shared library.

labs.takeaway: Open-ended investigation needs a dynamic plan that adapts to findings; fixed pipelines cannot follow new leads.

labs.title: Regulatory digest sometimes drops deadlines
labs.context: A research system produces a monthly regulatory digest for six jurisdictions, and each one must always cover the same four items: new rules, open consultations, enforcement actions and upcoming deadlines. The coordinator plans every run dynamically, and in about 1 run in 6 a jurisdiction silently loses its deadlines section.
labs.question: What change best guarantees complete digests?

options.text: Replace dynamic planning with a fixed pipeline that runs the same four research steps for each jurisdiction, then assembles the digest.
options.code:
for_each: [UK, EU, US, SG, AU, CA]
steps:
  - new_rules
  - open_consultations
  - enforcement_actions
  - upcoming_deadlines
then: assemble_digest

trace.text: Pipeline: 6 jurisdictions x 4 fixed steps = 24 tasks.
Deadlines step runs for all 6 jurisdictions.
Digest assembled from 24 results.
Twelve months later: no missing sections.

options.verdict: All four items, every jurisdiction, every month.
options.why: Predictable work with mandatory aspects suits a fixed sequential pipeline, which runs every step every time. Dynamic planning suits open-ended work, not a checklist.

options.text: Add a line to the coordinator prompt reminding it that all four items are mandatory for every jurisdiction.
options.code:
Coordinator prompt addition:
"IMPORTANT: every jurisdiction MUST include new
rules, consultations, enforcement and deadlines."

trace.text: Reminder added to the coordinator prompt.
Plans 23 of 24 tasks for this month.
Singapore digest has no deadlines section.

options.verdict: Misses become rarer, not impossible.
options.why: Probabilistic where the stem needs a guarantee. The coordinator still plans each run itself, so a section can still be skipped.

options.text: Give the dynamic coordinator a larger iteration budget, so it has time to reach every item in every jurisdiction.

trace.text: Budget raised from 60 to 120 iterations.
Uses 74 iterations; plans no deadlines task for Canada.
Canada digest incomplete; cost up 20%.

options.verdict: More time, same skipped step.
options.why: Trap: an open-ended agent with a bigger budget for work whose aspects are always the same. The skips come from planning, not from running out of time.

options.text: Add a reviewer agent that reads each finished digest and reruns the whole month if any section is missing.

trace.text: Reviewer: "EU deadlines missing."
Whole month rerun: 24 more tasks.
Digest a day late; research cost doubled this month.

options.verdict: Catches gaps late and expensively.
options.why: Over-engineered: it detects the miss after the fact and repeats all 24 tasks to fix one. A fixed pipeline prevents the miss in the first place.

labs.takeaway: Predictable, mandatory steps belong in a fixed pipeline; save dynamic planning for open-ended work.

checks.q: Every PR must be checked for the same four aspects. Fixed pipeline or adaptive agent?
checks.a: A fixed sequential pipeline (prompt chaining), because the steps are predictable and mandatory.

checks.q: What problem does a separate cross-file integration pass solve?
checks.a: It catches issues that span files, such as a renamed function still called elsewhere, which per-file passes cannot see.

checks.q: How should a plan for "add tests to a legacy codebase" be built?
checks.a: Map the structure, identify high-impact areas, build a prioritised plan, and adapt it as dependencies are discovered.

quiz.q: A 20-file pull request is reviewed in one pass, and later files get only brief comments. What is the best fix?
options: Use a longer, more detailed prompt that asks for care on every file
Run per-file local passes, then a separate cross-file integration pass
Run per-file passes in parallel and merge their findings at the end
Give an open-ended review agent a larger token budget for the job
quiz.why: One pass dilutes attention across files. Per-file passes give focus, and the integration pass catches what spans files.

quiz.q: Per-file reviews pass, but the build breaks because a renamed function is still called elsewhere. What was missing?
options: A stricter per-file prompt that checks every function call for typos
A fixed pipeline that checks security before performance in each file
A separate integration pass over interfaces and call sites across files
A single combined review of all the files in one long prompt instead
quiz.why: A single file cannot show a broken caller in another file. The separate integration pass exists to catch cross-file problems.

quiz.q: Every PR must always be checked for security, error handling and performance. Which decomposition fits?
options: A fixed pipeline, because the steps are predictable and mandatory
Dynamic adaptive decomposition, so the agent decides which checks matter
An open-ended agent with a larger budget so it can cover more aspects
A single pass that asks for all three aspects in one detailed prompt
quiz.why: Prompt chaining guarantees every mandatory aspect runs. An open-ended agent might skip one, whatever its budget.

quiz.q: A team must add tests to an unfamiliar legacy codebase. How should the work be planned?
options: Write a complete, fixed test plan on day one and follow it in order
Run the same fixed pipeline of test steps on every module in turn
Ask Claude to write tests for every file in one single large pass
Map the code, find high-impact areas, then adapt a prioritised plan
quiz.why: Open-ended work needs dynamic decomposition. The plan should change as dependencies are discovered.

misconceptions.myth: A longer, more careful prompt fixes a review that misses issues.
misconceptions.fact: The problem is diluted attention across files. Per-file passes plus a separate integration pass fix it.

misconceptions.myth: Per-file reviews cover everything if each one is thorough.
misconceptions.fact: A single file cannot show a broken caller in another file. Cross-file problems need their own integration pass.

misconceptions.myth: An open-ended agent is always more capable than a fixed pipeline.
misconceptions.fact: For predictable, mandatory checks a fixed pipeline is more reliable, because every step is guaranteed to run.

scenario.title: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenario.story:
A payments team ran Claude Code in CI to review every pull request. One prompt reviewed the whole diff for bugs, security and style. On small PRs it worked well. On a 15-file PR that renamed `getUser` to `fetchUser`, it left detailed notes on the first four files and one-liners on the rest. It missed a SQL injection in file 11, and the merged build failed because file 14 still called `getUser`.

Their first idea was a longer prompt: "Be extremely thorough on every file." The next large PR showed the same pattern.

They restructured the job instead. A fixed chain of aspects (security, error handling, performance) now runs per file, with files reviewed in parallel. Then a separate integration pass receives only a summary of exports, signatures and call sites, and looks for mismatches between files.

On the next rename PR, a per-file pass flagged an injection and the integration pass flagged a stale call. Both reached the author before merge.

plain: Long jobs often span several sessions. You can **resume** an earlier session to pick up where you left off, **start fresh** with a short structured summary, or **fork** a session to try two ideas side by side. The choice depends on how much of the earlier work is still accurate and whether you are comparing options.
analogy: Coming back to a half-read book: if little has changed, you open it at your bookmark. If it is a new edition, you start the new copy with your notes. If you want to compare two endings, you photocopy the book at the same page and read each ending separately.

sections.h: Three options: resume, fresh start, fork
sections.body:
**You can continue an old session, start clean with a summary, or branch into separate copies.**

- **Resume** (`--resume <session-name>`): continue a named earlier session. Claude keeps its old context, including past tool results such as file contents and test output.
- **Fresh session with an injected structured summary**: start clean, and paste in a short, structured record of what matters, such as decisions, findings and next steps.
- **Fork** (`fork_session`): create an **independent branch** from a shared starting point. Each branch carries on separately and cannot see the other.

All three keep useful work. They differ in how much old context they carry, and whether that old context still helps or now misleads.

sections.h: How to choose, step by step
sections.body:
**Ask how much has changed, then ask whether you are comparing options.**

1. **Is the earlier context mostly still valid?**
   - Yes → **resume**.
   - No, most earlier tool results are out of date → **fresh session plus a structured summary**.
2. **If resuming, say what changed.** For example: "Since last time, `auth.py` and `session.py` changed." Claude then re-reads just those files, which is **targeted re-analysis**, instead of exploring the whole codebase again.
3. **Are you comparing alternatives?** Build the shared analysis once, then **fork** one branch per approach, for example unit-tests-first against integration-tests-first.

In exam stems, one line usually says how much has changed or that two approaches are being compared. That line decides the answer.

sections.h: How each option looks in practice
sections.body:
**Each choice maps to a concrete command or option.**

- **Resume in Claude Code**: `claude --resume auth-refactor`, then tell it which files changed.
- **Fresh start**: open a new session and give it a summary with clear headings, for example:
  - *Decisions*: tokens move to httpOnly cookies
  - *Open issues*: #14 CSRF, #17 expiry
  - *Files in scope*: `src/auth.py`, `src/session.py`
  - *Next step*: fix #14
- **Fork in the Agent SDK**: `ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=baseline_id, fork_session=True)` in Python, or `resume` with `forkSession: true` in TypeScript. The fork gets a new session ID and the baseline stays untouched.

A structured summary beats a prose recap because each key fact has its own slot and cannot quietly drop out.

**Each option has a clear case where it does harm.**

- **Do not resume** when most earlier tool results are out of date. Claude will trust old file contents and old test results, and act on them.
- **Do not start from scratch** when only a few files changed. Re-exploring everything wastes time and tokens. Resume and name the changed files.
- **Do not compare approaches one after another in one session.** The second attempt has seen the first one's code, conclusions and mistakes, so the comparison is not fair. Fork instead.
- **Do not inject a loose prose recap.** "We looked at some auth stuff and it seemed mostly fine" loses the facts that matter. Use a structured summary.

**The failures are acting on stale context, wasting work, and biased comparisons.**

- A team resumes a two-week-old session after a big refactor. Claude edits functions that no longer exist.
- A developer changes two files, starts a new session and asks Claude to "understand the codebase" again. Forty minutes go on re-reading unchanged code.
- An engineer tries strategy A, then says "now try strategy B" in the same session. B quietly reuses A's helpers, so the comparison is skewed.
- A fresh session gets a chatty paragraph instead of a summary. Which tests fail, and which decision was made, are both missing.

The rule: **mostly valid → resume and name the changed files; stale → fresh session with a structured summary; comparing → fork.**

example.title: Worked example: resuming, forking and a structured summary
example.code:
# Resume yesterday's named session; most context is still valid
claude --resume auth-refactor
# then tell it what changed:
#   "Since last session, src/auth.py and src/session.py changed.
#    Re-analyse only those and update your findings."

# Context is stale (big refactor merged): start fresh with a summary
claude -p "$(cat summary.md)

Continue the auth review from this summary."

# summary.md (structured):
#   ## Decisions: tokens move to httpOnly cookies
#   ## Findings: 2 open issues (#14 CSRF, #17 expiry)
#   ## Files in scope: src/auth.py, src/session.py
#   ## Next step: fix #14

# Compare two test strategies from the same baseline (SDK, illustrative):
#   options = ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=baseline_id, fork_session=True)
notes: `--resume auth-refactor` continues a named session when its context is still mostly right.
Naming the changed files enables targeted re-analysis instead of a full re-exploration.
When context is stale, a fresh session gets a structured summary with clear headings, not a prose recap.
Forking from a shared baseline gives each strategy an independent branch. The SDK line is illustrative.

labs.title: Compare two testing strategies fairly
labs.context: Claude spent 90 minutes analysing a legacy module in a named session, and that analysis is still valid. The team now wants to compare a unit-tests-first plan with an integration-tests-first plan. Each plan must be judged without influence from the other.
labs.question: How should they run the comparison?

options.text: Ask for both plans in the existing session, one after the other, then ask Claude which of the two approaches is better.
options.code:
Session "legacy-tests":
> "Write a unit-test-first plan and draft tests."
> "Now do the same with integration tests first."
> "Which approach is better?"

trace.text: Unit-first plan: creates mock helpers and fixtures.
Integration-first plan: reuses the mock helpers from the first attempt.
"Integration-first was quicker to write."
Comparison biased: the second attempt built on the first.

options.verdict: Second approach contaminated by the first.
options.why: In one session the second plan is influenced by the first, so the comparison is biased. Trap: comparing alternatives sequentially instead of using fork_session for independent branches.

options.text: Start two fresh sessions, each re-analysing the module from scratch and then writing one of the two plans.
options.code:
Session A (new):
  "Analyse the module, then plan unit-first."
Session B (new):
  "Analyse the module, then plan integration-first."

trace.text: Session A: re-reads 40 files to rebuild the analysis.
Session B: re-reads the same 40 files.
Analyses differ slightly, so the baseline is not shared.
Independent, but wasteful and less comparable.

options.verdict: Independent, but duplicated work and no shared baseline.
options.why: The stem says the 90-minute analysis is still valid, so redoing it twice wastes effort and the two plans no longer share a baseline. Trap: starting from scratch when the context is still valid.

options.text: Use fork_session to branch twice from the analysed session, ask each branch for one plan, then compare.
options.code:
Baseline session: module analysed once.
Fork 1 (fork_session): "Plan unit-tests-first."
Fork 2 (fork_session): "Plan integration-tests-first."
Compare the two outputs.

trace.text: Baseline analysis exists (done once).
fork_session -> branch 1 and branch 2 from the same point.
Branch 1: unit-first plan, no knowledge of branch 2.
Branch 2: integration-first plan, no knowledge of branch 1.
Fair comparison from an identical starting point.

options.verdict: Fair, independent comparison with no repeated analysis.
options.why: `fork_session` creates independent branches from a shared analysis baseline, which is exactly the case for comparing alternatives. The valid analysis is reused, not repeated.

options.text: Resume the named session for the unit-first plan, then resume the same session again later for the integration-first plan.
options.code:
claude --resume legacy-tests
> "Plan unit-tests-first."
# next day
claude --resume legacy-tests
> "Now plan integration-tests-first."

trace.text: --resume legacy-tests -> unit-first plan written.
--resume legacy-tests (later) -> history includes the unit-first plan.
Integration-first plan reuses the unit-first fixtures.
Comparison biased, as in a single session.

options.verdict: Second plan still sees the first.
options.why: Resuming twice continues one history, so the second plan is written with the first in context. Trap: resume keeps context; only a fork gives an independent branch.

labs.takeaway: Comparing alternatives from a shared baseline: fork_session, not one session or two fresh ones.

labs.title: Returning customer after ten days of changes
labs.context: A support agent keeps a named session for each complex billing dispute. A customer returns 10 days later, after a refund has posted, a replacement has shipped and the refund policy has changed, so most earlier tool results are stale. The customer must not be asked to repeat anything.
labs.question: How should the agent continue the case?

options.text: Resume the named session, so Claude keeps every earlier tool result and the full conversation history.

trace.text: Session resumed with 10-day-old tool results.
"Did my refund go through?"
"Your refund is still pending; under our 14-day policy..."
Wrong on both counts: refund posted, policy now 30 days.

options.verdict: Answers from 10-day-old data.
options.why: Trap: resuming when most prior tool results are stale. The old results say the refund is pending and the old policy applies, and Claude trusts them.

options.text: Start a new session and inject a structured summary: customer ID, order IDs, what was promised, and the open questions to re-check.
options.code:
{
  "customer_id": "C-4410",
  "orders": ["8812", "8813"],
  "promised": ["refund 8812", "replacement 8813"],
  "recheck": ["refund status", "replacement delivery",
              "current refund policy"]
}

trace.text: New session with summary: C-4410, orders 8812/8813, promised refund + replacement.
tool_use: lookup_order(8812) -> refund posted 3 days ago
tool_use: lookup_order(8813) -> replacement delivered
"Your refund posted on Monday and the replacement arrived. Anything else?"

options.verdict: Fresh data, nothing asked twice.
options.why: When prior tool results are stale, start fresh with an injected structured summary. The key facts carry over, and the agent re-checks current state with its tools.

options.text: Start a new session with no prior context and let the agent call its tools again to rebuild the picture.

trace.text: New empty session.
"Could you tell me your order numbers and what happened?"
"I explained all this 10 days ago."

scenario.title: Developer Productivity with Claude
scenario.story:
A developer spent Monday with Claude Code analysing a legacy billing module, in a session named `billing-tests`. On Tuesday a teammate changed two files. On Wednesday a large refactor moved half the module into a new package.

On Tuesday the developer ran `claude --resume billing-tests` and said, "Since yesterday, `invoice.py` and `tax.py` changed. Re-check only those." Claude re-read two files instead of forty and updated its notes in minutes.

Wednesday was different. Most earlier file reads were now wrong. Rather than resume, the developer started a new session with a structured summary: decisions made, open issues, files in scope and the next step.

Then the team wanted to compare unit-tests-first with integration-tests-first. A first try in one session was biased, because the second plan reused the first plan's mocks. So they built the analysis once and used `fork_session` to create two independent branches. Both plans started from the same point, and the comparison was fair.
